questions.q: A support-resolution agent must look up orders, check policy, and draft refunds. Requests follow a predictable sequence. Best architecture?
opts: Fully autonomous agent with 30 tools
Prompt chaining / fixed workflow with tool calls at defined steps
Ten parallel agents voting
One giant prompt with all data inline
questions.exp: When the sequence is known, encode it. A fixed workflow with tool calls at defined steps is cheaper, faster, and far easier to test and debug, because the path is the same every run and a failure happens somewhere you can point at. Autonomy earns its cost only when the path genuinely cannot be specified ahead of time. The architectural discipline here is to reach for the simplest control flow that covers the requirement and escalate on evidence - reaching for an agent because the domain feels sophisticated is how teams pay loop cost and unpredictability for a pipeline they could have written.
why: Thirty tools and full autonomy buys open-endedness this task does not need, and pays for it in cost, latency and unpredictability.
Correct. A predictable sequence belongs in a fixed workflow with tool calls at defined steps - cheaper, faster and testable.
Voting is for problems with genuine uncertainty about the answer. Here the steps are known, so parallel agents multiply cost for nothing.
Inlining all the data abandons the tools that make the lookups accurate and current, and scales badly as the data grows.

questions.q: When is an orchestrator-workers (multi-agent) pattern justified over a single agent?
opts: Always — more agents, more power
When subtasks are separable, benefit from isolated contexts, or can run in parallel (e.g., broad research)
When latency must be minimal
When you want to save tokens
questions.exp: Orchestrator-workers earns its overhead when subtasks are genuinely separable: each worker gets an isolated context so the main thread does not fill with intermediate reading, and independent branches can run in parallel. Broad research is the archetype. What it costs is coordination, and each worker re-establishes its own context before it can start - so it increases token spend rather than saving it, and adds latency on any task that was really sequential. Use it where the work genuinely fans out, not because a task feels large.
why: More agents means more coordination, more tokens and more failure modes. It is a trade to make deliberately rather than a default.
Correct. Separable subtasks that benefit from isolated contexts or can run in parallel, which is exactly the shape of broad research.
Coordination adds latency. A single agent is generally faster when the work is sequential anyway.
Each worker re-establishes its own context, so this pattern usually costs more tokens rather than fewer.

questions.q: Your agent loop occasionally spirals, repeating the same failing tool call. The architectural fix is:
opts: Bigger model
Loop guards: max iterations, repeated-failure detection, and an escalation/fallback path
Remove the tool
Retry forever silently
questions.exp: A spiralling loop needs bounds, not capability. Cap iterations, detect repeated identical failures, and define an escalation path so the run ends in a recoverable state rather than simply stopping. The detection matters as much as the cap: a loop that retries the same failing call twenty times burns the whole budget before the ceiling fires, whereas noticing the repetition ends it in three. A more capable model can spiral just as thoroughly. Removing the tool discards a capability over a control problem, and silent retries turn a visible failure into a hang.
why: Capability does not bound iteration. A stronger model can repeat the same failing call just as persistently.
Correct. Iteration caps, repeated-failure detection and a defined escalation path, so the loop is bounded and ends recoverably.
Removing the tool loses a capability to solve a control-flow problem that guards would fix directly.
Silent unbounded retries turn a visible failure into a hang and consume the entire budget on one broken call.

questions.q: In a routing architecture, an initial classifier sends queries to specialized handlers. The main benefit is:
opts: It eliminates hallucinations
Each handler gets a focused prompt/tools for its category, improving quality and cost per query type
It avoids using the API
Users see more options
questions.exp: Routing lets each handler carry a focused prompt and a minimal tool set for its category, which improves quality and lets you match cost to difficulty - simple categories run on a cheaper tier while hard ones get capability. A single handler covering everything has to carry every instruction and every tool on every request, which dilutes the prompt and inflates cost. What routing does not do is remove hallucination or reduce API usage; it adds a classification step, so the gain is specialisation rather than fewer calls.
why: Routing directs a query to a better-suited handler. It does nothing about whether that handler's answer is factually right.
Correct. Each handler gets a focused prompt and tool set for its category, which improves quality and lets cost match difficulty.
Routing adds a classification call. It increases API usage rather than avoiding it.
Routing is internal architecture and is normally invisible to the user.

questions.q: An agent must decide between acting autonomously vs. asking the user. Sensitive irreversible actions (deleting data, sending emails) should:
opts: Be fully autonomous for speed
Require human confirmation / approval gates
Be silently logged only
Be disabled entirely always
questions.exp: Irreversible actions need a human in the loop, because the cost of being wrong is not recoverable and an agent's action sequence is decided at run time - you cannot enumerate in advance everything it might attempt. Approval gates are also what limit the damage from prompt injection: the injected text only becomes an incident if the agent can act on it unsupervised. Note the answer is a gate rather than a ban: disabling these capabilities entirely removes real value, and the point is to require confirmation rather than to prevent the action.
why: Speed is the wrong optimisation on an action that cannot be undone, and unsupervised irreversible actions are what turn an injection into an incident.
Correct. Human confirmation before irreversible actions, which bounds both mistakes and successful manipulation.
Logging records what happened after the fact. The data is already deleted or the email already sent.
A blanket ban removes genuine value. The control is a gate on the action rather than removal of the capability.

questions.q: Your team wants consistent Claude Code behavior across all engineers on a repo. Best mechanism?
opts: Verbal team norms
A checked-in CLAUDE.md with conventions, commands, and guardrails
Each dev's private notes
Longer chat sessions
questions.exp: A checked-in CLAUDE.md puts the conventions where the tooling reads them and where review applies, so every engineer's session starts from the same instructions and a change goes through the same process as any other repository change. That is what makes it consistent rather than merely documented. Verbal norms and private notes both live outside the repository, so they drift, and neither is loaded into anyone's session automatically. Longer chat sessions address none of this and tend to degrade as context accumulates.
why: Verbal norms are not loaded into anyone's session and drift as the team changes. Nothing enforces them.
Correct. A checked-in file puts conventions where the tooling reads them and where code review applies to changes.
Private notes are per-person by definition, which is the inconsistency you are trying to remove.
Session length has no bearing on shared conventions, and long sessions tend to lose earlier context anyway.

questions.q: For a large refactor, the recommended Claude Code workflow is:
opts: One giant 'refactor everything' prompt
Plan first (explore/plan mode), review the plan, then execute in steps with verification (tests) between
Disable tests to go faster
Let it run unattended overnight
questions.exp: Plan, review, then execute in verified steps. The review is the load-bearing part: a plan is cheap to correct and a completed wrong refactor is expensive, so the moment to catch a misunderstanding is before any code changes. Verification between steps then keeps errors local rather than letting them compound across a large change. One giant prompt gives you no checkpoint and no way to localise a failure. Disabling tests removes the signal that makes stepwise execution safe, and running unattended on a large refactor removes the review entirely.
why: A single sweeping prompt offers no checkpoint, so a misunderstanding surfaces only after everything has changed.
Correct. Plan, review the plan, then execute in steps with verification between - so errors stay local and cheap to fix.
Tests are the signal that makes stepwise execution safe. Disabling them removes the check that catches a wrong step.
Unattended execution on a large refactor removes the review at exactly the point where it is most valuable.

questions.q: Claude Code subagents are useful primarily because they:
opts: Are cheaper per token
Run tasks in separate context windows, keeping the main session focused and enabling parallel work
Have different training data
Skip permissions
questions.exp: Subagents run in separate context windows, which keeps the main session focused and lets independent work proceed in parallel. Only the result returns, so the main thread does not fill with the subagent's intermediate reading and tool output. That is a real architectural gain on work that fans out. It is not a cost saving - each subagent re-establishes its own context first - and it is not a capability or permission change, since a subagent runs the same models under the same rules as the session that spawned it.
why: Each subagent re-establishes its own context, so delegation generally increases token spend rather than reducing it.
Correct. Separate context windows keep the main session focused and let independent work run in parallel.
Subagents run the same models. Isolation changes what they see, not what they know.
Permissions apply to subagents as they do to the main session. Delegation is not an escalation path.

questions.q: To let Claude Code run repository tests automatically before declaring work done, you would:
opts: Trust it remembers
Encode the requirement in CLAUDE.md and/or use hooks to run tests on completion
Run tests manually a week later
Avoid tests in agentic workflows
questions.exp: Encode the requirement where the tooling enforces it: state it in CLAUDE.md so it applies to every session, and use hooks where you want it to run automatically rather than depending on the model choosing to. The distinction matters - an instruction is followed most of the time, while a hook runs every time - so anything you genuinely require belongs in the mechanism rather than the prompt. Trusting recall gives you neither. Deferring tests to a later manual pass discards the fast feedback that makes agentic work safe, and skipping them removes the check entirely.
why: Nothing persists between sessions unless it is written down where the tooling reads it.
Correct. State it in CLAUDE.md so it applies every session, and use hooks where it must run rather than merely be requested.
A week-late manual run discards the fast feedback that keeps agentic changes correctable while they are still fresh.
Tests matter more in agentic workflows, not less, because more change is being made with less line-by-line attention.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline needs machine-parseable output with exact fields. The architect's choice:
opts: Free-form text and a regex parser
Schema-constrained structured output (or a tool with strict input schema), validated downstream
Ask for 'mostly JSON'
Markdown tables
questions.exp: Constrain the output shape at the request level and validate downstream. A schema makes the model generate against your structure rather than being asked for it, and validation in your code is where the guarantee actually lives. Free-form text with a regex parser is the failure profile to avoid: it works until the formatting drifts, and it fails by producing a subtly wrong value rather than an obvious error. Asking for mostly JSON invites exactly that drift, and Markdown tables are a presentation format that still needs parsing.
why: Regex over free text breaks on formatting drift, and it fails by extracting a subtly wrong value rather than erroring clearly.
Correct. Constrain the shape with a schema, then validate downstream so the guarantee lives in your code.
Mostly JSON is the worst target available - close enough to pass testing, loose enough to break in production.
Markdown tables are for presentation. They still need parsing and carry no structural guarantee.

questions.q: A prompt performs well on easy inputs but fails on edge cases. Best improvement strategy?
opts: Add few-shot examples covering the failing edge cases and explicit rules for them
Make the prompt shorter
Raise temperature
Switch providers
questions.exp: A failing edge case is a specification gap. Show the case as a worked example and state the rule that governs it, so the behaviour is both demonstrated and generalised - examples are the strongest signal in a prompt, and one that covers the awkward case teaches far more than a paragraph describing it. Shortening the prompt removes information when the problem is missing information. Sampling parameters are rejected on current models and never governed correctness anyway. Switching providers carries the same unstated edge case somewhere else.
why: Correct. Few-shot examples covering the failing cases plus explicit rules, so the behaviour is demonstrated and generalised.
Shortening removes information. An underspecified edge case needs more specification, not less.
Sampling parameters are rejected on current models, and they never governed correctness on edge cases in any case.
The gap is in the prompt rather than the provider. The same unstated case will fail elsewhere too.

questions.q: For a multi-pass review loop (draft → critique → revise), the main architectural benefit is:
opts: Fewer tokens used
Quality gains from self-review catching errors a single pass misses
It removes the need for tests
Faster responses
questions.exp: A critique pass catches errors the drafting pass missed, because reviewing and generating are different tasks and a fresh look at finished text surfaces problems that were invisible while producing it. That is the whole benefit, and it is a real one on work where quality matters more than latency. Everything else moves the wrong way: multiple passes cost more tokens and take longer. Note self-review is weaker than independent verification, so it complements tests and human review rather than substituting for them.
why: Multiple passes cost more tokens, not fewer. The gain is quality, paid for in spend.
Correct. Self-review catches errors a single pass misses, because reviewing and generating are different tasks.
Self-review is weaker than independent verification and does not replace tests or human review.
Additional passes add latency. This trades speed for quality rather than improving both.

questions.q: You need Claude's response to be valid JSON matching a fixed schema. On current Claude models, the correct mechanism is:
opts: Prefilling the assistant turn with "{" so generation continues as JSON
Structured outputs — a schema via output_config.format, or a tool with a strict input schema
Asking for JSON in the system prompt and repairing the output with a regex
Setting a stop sequence at "}" and retrying on parse failures
questions.exp: Structured outputs are the supported mechanism on current models: a schema via output_config.format, or a tool with a strict input schema. Prefilling the assistant turn was the older technique and is now rejected with a 400, so code carrying it forward fails outright rather than degrading quietly - which is worth knowing when migrating. Asking in the system prompt and repairing with a regex produces valid JSON most of the time, the worst possible failure rate. A stop sequence on a closing brace truncates any nested object at its first inner brace.
why: Prefill is rejected with a 400 on current models, so this fails validation rather than producing constrained output.
Correct. A schema via output_config.format, or a tool with a strict input schema, so conformance comes from the request.
This is correct often enough to pass review and wrong often enough to break in production, which is the worst failure profile available.
A stop sequence on a closing brace cuts at the first one, truncating any nested object partway through.

questions.q: You're designing tools for an agent. Which principle applies?
opts: Many overlapping micro-tools are best
Few, well-named, clearly documented tools with distinct purposes and strict schemas
Tools should share one generic 'do_anything' endpoint
Descriptions waste tokens
questions.exp: Few, well-named tools with distinct purposes and strict schemas. The description is what the model reasons over when choosing, so clarity there matters more than coverage - and overlapping micro-tools create near-miss selections between options that all look plausible. Every tool also costs context on every request, so a large surface degrades the decision it was meant to enable. A single generic endpoint pushes the dispatch problem into free-text arguments where no schema can constrain it, which is the worst of both worlds.
why: Overlapping tools create near-miss selections between plausible options, and each one costs context on every request.
Correct. Few, clearly documented tools with distinct purposes and strict schemas, since the description drives selection.
A generic endpoint moves dispatch into free-text arguments where no schema can constrain it.
Descriptions are the primary input to tool selection. Cutting them degrades exactly the decision you need to be right.

questions.q: A tool can return 10,000 rows. The agent only ever needs a handful. Design the tool to:
opts: Return everything for completeness
Support filtering/pagination and return concise, relevant results to protect the context window
Return a file path only
Fail if results exceed 100
questions.exp: Design the tool to filter and paginate, and return concise results. Context is the scarce resource in an agentic system: ten thousand rows crowd out the reasoning the agent needs to do, cost tokens on every subsequent turn of the loop, and bury the handful of rows that mattered. Push the selection into the tool where code can do it precisely and cheaply. Returning only a file path defers the problem without solving it, and a hard failure above a threshold turns a manageable case into a broken one.
why: Completeness at the cost of the context window is a bad trade - the relevant rows get buried and every later turn pays for the rest.
Correct. Filtering and pagination keep results concise, which protects the context the agent needs for reasoning.
A path defers the problem to another step rather than solving it, and the agent still has to read the contents somehow.
Failing above a threshold converts a manageable large result into a broken call, when pagination would have handled it.

questions.q: When should you wrap a capability as an MCP server instead of a bespoke in-app tool?
opts: Never — MCP is only for Anthropic products
When multiple clients/agents should reuse it through a standard interface
Only for databases
When you need lower latency than function calls
questions.exp: Wrap it as an MCP server when several clients or agents should reuse the same capability through a standard interface. That is the reuse-and-versioning argument: the server evolves on its own release cycle and any MCP-aware client can consume it, which turns an integration into shared infrastructure. For a capability only one application will ever use, an in-app tool is simpler and has fewer moving parts. Note the trade-off - a server adds a process boundary and therefore latency, so it is not the faster option.
why: MCP is an open standard with implementations well beyond Anthropic's own products.
Correct. When several clients or agents should reuse the capability through a standard interface, which makes it shared infrastructure.
Servers can expose any capability - filesystems, APIs, internal services - not only databases.
A server adds a process boundary and therefore latency. It is chosen for reuse, not for speed.

questions.q: An MCP server exposes a 'run_sql' tool for analytics. The safest design is:
opts: Full read-write on production
Read-only access to a replica, query allowlists/limits, and audit logging
Root credentials for flexibility
No limits — the model is careful
questions.exp: Read-only access to a replica, with query allowlists or limits and audit logging. Each control covers a different failure: the replica protects production from load and from writes, allowlists and limits bound what any single query can do, and logging tells you afterwards what was actually run. Together they mean a manipulated or mistaken query cannot damage live data. The reasoning matters more than the checklist - an agent's queries are generated at run time, so you cannot enumerate them in advance, which is why the boundary has to be structural rather than a matter of care.
why: Write access to production means one manipulated or mistaken query damages live data with nothing to stop it.
Correct. A read-only replica, query allowlists and limits, and audit logging - each covering a different failure mode.
Root credentials remove every boundary at once, which is the opposite of what an agent-facing tool needs.
Care is not a control. Queries are generated at run time, so the boundary has to be structural rather than behavioural.

questions.q: A long-running agent gradually forgets early constraints. Architectural mitigation?
opts: Hope for the best
Compaction: periodically summarize state/decisions into a durable note re-injected into context
Restart and lose everything
Raise temperature
questions.exp: Compaction is the architectural answer: periodically distil the decisions, constraints and state that still matter into a durable note and re-inject that, rather than carrying the whole transcript. It keeps what is load-bearing prominent while dropping superseded drafts and resolved tangents, which is exactly what a growing agent context buries. Do it proactively at a utilisation threshold with headroom left for the summarisation call itself - waiting for a failure means discovering the problem when there is no room left to fix it.
why: Drift is predictable rather than exceptional. Every long-running agent hits it without a deliberate mechanism.
Correct. Periodically summarise state and decisions into a durable note that is re-injected, keeping what matters prominent.
Restarting without carrying state forward discards the work, which is the failure compaction exists to prevent.
Sampling parameters do not affect context retention, and current models reject them regardless.

questions.q: Which is a signal you should retrieve context just-in-time rather than preload everything?
opts: Corpus far exceeds the context window and most content is irrelevant per query
The corpus is 2 pages
Latency doesn't matter
You enjoy large bills
questions.exp: Retrieve just in time when the corpus far exceeds the window and most of it is irrelevant per query. Both halves matter: if everything fits, preloading is simpler and avoids a retrieval step that can itself fail; if most content were relevant to every query, selection would buy little. When both hold, retrieval cuts cost and improves focus at once. The trade-off to watch is retrieval quality, since a question whose answer spans distant sections can be under-served - the ceiling on a retrieval system is usually set by what it fetches rather than by the model reading it.
why: Correct. A corpus far exceeding the window with most content irrelevant per query is exactly the case selection pays off.
Two pages fit comfortably. Adding retrieval there is complexity and a failure mode for no benefit.
Latency tolerance is unrelated to whether the corpus fits or how much of it is relevant.
Cost is a reason to retrieve rather than preload, so this states the situation backwards.

questions.q: To make an agent pipeline resilient to a model outage or degraded responses, an architect plans:
opts: Nothing — outages are rare
Fallbacks: retries with backoff, model fallback tiers, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation paths
A status page
Blaming the vendor
questions.exp: Resilience is a set of layered controls rather than one mechanism: retries with backoff for transient failures, fallback tiers when a model is unavailable, circuit breakers so a failing dependency stops being called, and a defined degraded path so the system does something sensible when none of it works. That last one is the piece people leave out, and it is what separates a graceful degradation from an outage. Rarity is not an argument - outages are rare and consequential, which is the standard case for designing around them.
why: Rare and consequential is the standard case for designing around something rather than for ignoring it.
Correct. Retries with backoff, fallback tiers, circuit breakers and a defined degraded path - layered controls covering different failures.
A status page communicates an outage. It does nothing to keep the pipeline working through one.
Attribution does not restore service, and the user experience is the same either way.

questions.q: Where should deterministic logic (date math, exact totals, ID validation) live in an agentic system?
opts: In the model's prompt as instructions
In code/tools — let the model orchestrate, let code compute
In the model's memory
Nowhere
questions.exp: Deterministic work belongs in code. Date arithmetic, exact totals and identifier validation have correct answers that a function computes reliably every time, whereas a model produces them plausibly - and plausibly wrong arithmetic is the kind of error that survives review because it looks reasonable. Let the model orchestrate and let code compute. This is the clearest division of labour in agentic design: use the model for judgement, ambiguity and language, and give it tools for anything with a definite answer.
why: Instructions ask the model to compute rather than giving it a reliable way to. Plausibly wrong arithmetic survives review because it looks reasonable.
Correct. Deterministic work belongs in code and tools - the model orchestrates, code computes.
There is no persistent memory that performs computation. This misplaces both the mechanism and the responsibility.
The logic is required. The question is where it lives, and code is the only place it can be reliable.

questions.q: Two agents in your system communicate by passing entire conversation histories to each other. Costs explode. Better pattern?
opts: Pass distilled, structured summaries/artifacts between agents instead of raw transcripts
Bigger context windows
Compress with zip
Merge into one agent with double context
questions.exp: Pass distilled artifacts rather than raw transcripts. A structured summary carries the conclusions and the state the next agent actually needs, while a full history carries every intermediate step it does not - and at each hop the cost compounds, because the receiving agent pays for all of it and then adds its own. Designing the interface between agents is a real architectural decision, and treating the transcript as the interface is the default that causes this. Larger windows and compression both make the symptom affordable for slightly longer without addressing it.
why: Correct. Pass distilled summaries and artifacts, so each agent receives the conclusions it needs rather than every intermediate step.
A larger window raises the ceiling without reducing what you send. The cost per hop is unchanged.
Compression is invisible to the model - the content is tokenised as text either way, so nothing is saved.
Merging discards the isolation that made separate agents worthwhile, and doubles the context every turn carries.

questions.q: You need consistent tone/policy across 40 different prompts in a product. The maintainable approach is:
opts: Copy-paste the policy into each prompt
A shared, versioned system-prompt component included by all prompts
Trust each author
Fine-tune per prompt
questions.exp: A shared, versioned system-prompt component included by all forty prompts. One definition means a policy change propagates everywhere at once and review applies to a single place, which is exactly the property copy-paste destroys: forty copies drift, and the drift is invisible until someone compares them. Trusting each author is the same problem stated as a hope. Fine-tuning per prompt is wildly disproportionate for shared tone and policy, and would need redoing for every future policy update.
why: Forty copies drift, and the drift is invisible until someone compares them. A single policy change means forty edits.
Correct. One shared, versioned component included everywhere, so a policy change propagates at once and review applies in one place.
Consistency by good intentions is the situation you are trying to fix, and new authors have nothing to follow.
Fine-tuning is disproportionate for shared tone and policy, and would need redoing on every future update.

questions.q: A CI pipeline uses Claude Code headlessly to fix lint errors on PRs. Critical safeguard?
opts: No safeguards; speed matters
Scoped permissions, no push to main, changes land as PR diffs a human reviews
Auto-merge everything green
Run as repo admin
questions.exp: Scope the permissions and land changes as reviewable diffs. Headless automation removes the human from the loop during execution, so the review has to move to the boundary - a pull request a person approves - and the permissions have to assume the automation may do something unintended. That reasoning holds regardless of how reliable the tool has been, because CI runs on untrusted input: a pull request's contents are attacker-controllable in an open repository, which makes injection a live concern rather than a theoretical one.
why: Speed without safeguards on an automated agent with repository write access is how a single bad run rewrites a codebase.
Correct. Scoped permissions, no direct push to main, and changes landing as diffs a human reviews.
Auto-merging on green removes the human review entirely, and passing lint is not evidence the change is correct.
Admin rights give the automation the broadest possible blast radius for any mistake or manipulation.

questions.q: Claude keeps calling a search tool when it should use the calculator. First fix to try?
opts: Delete the search tool
Sharpen both tool descriptions to state exactly when each should (and shouldn't) be used
Fine-tune the model
Add a third tool
questions.exp: Sharpen both descriptions. Tool selection is driven by what the descriptions say, so a wrong choice is usually a description problem - and stating when each tool should *not* be used is often what resolves it, because the confusion is at the boundary between them rather than within either one. Fix both sides, since the model is choosing between them. Deleting the search tool removes a capability to work around a wording issue. Fine-tuning is disproportionate, and a third tool adds another option to a decision that is already going wrong.
why: Deleting a capability to work around a description problem loses functionality the agent legitimately needs.
Correct. Sharpen both descriptions, including when each should not be used, since the confusion is at the boundary between them.
Fine-tuning is disproportionate for a tool-selection issue that clearer descriptions resolve directly.
Another tool adds a further option to a decision that is already being made badly.

questions.q: A task decomposes into four independent research questions whose answers are combined at the end. The fitting pattern is:
opts: A single sequential chain
Orchestrator with parallel workers, then a synthesis step
A router that picks one question
A human performing each step
questions.exp: Four independent questions combined at the end is the canonical fan-out shape: workers run in parallel with isolated contexts, and a synthesis step reconciles their findings. Independence is what makes it work - if the questions depended on each other, parallelism would buy nothing and the coordination would be pure overhead. The synthesis step is not optional either; without it you have four answers rather than one, and reconciling contradictions between workers is real work that someone has to do.
why: A sequential chain serialises work that could run at once, so total latency is the sum rather than the maximum.
Correct. Parallel workers on independent questions, then a synthesis step to reconcile and combine the findings.
Routing picks one path. All four questions need answering, so discarding three loses most of the task.
Manual execution abandons the automation entirely, and these are exactly the researchable subtasks worth delegating.

questions.q: Requests fall into three distinct categories, each best handled by a different prompt and model. The right pattern is:
opts: Run all three handlers and pick the best output
A routing step that classifies then dispatches to the specialist handler
One general prompt covering all three
A multi-agent debate
questions.exp: Classify then dispatch. A routing step costs one cheap call and lets each specialist carry a focused prompt, a minimal tool set, and a model matched to its difficulty - so quality goes up and cost tracks the category rather than the worst case. Running all three handlers triples the cost and then needs a judge to pick a winner, which is a harder problem than the original classification. One general prompt has to carry every instruction on every request, diluting all three. Debate is for genuine uncertainty about an answer, not for categorisation.
why: Running every handler triples cost and then needs a judge to choose, which is harder than the classification you avoided.
Correct. Classify once, then dispatch to a specialist with a focused prompt and a model matched to that category.
One prompt covering three categories carries every instruction on every request, which dilutes all three.
Debate suits genuine uncertainty about an answer. Category assignment is a classification problem with a cheap solution.

questions.q: The strongest argument for choosing a simpler orchestration than you think you need is:
opts: Simpler systems are always more accurate
Every added layer adds cost, latency, and failure surface, and must earn its place
Complex systems are harder to explain to customers
Simple systems use newer models
questions.exp: Every layer costs something on every run - tokens, latency, and a new way to fail - so it has to earn its place against a simpler alternative. That framing is what keeps architecture honest, because the pull is always toward more structure: an extra agent or validation pass feels like diligence, and each one is paid for continuously. Simplicity is not automatically more accurate, which is worth being precise about; the argument is about cost, debuggability and failure surface, and a complex system that genuinely earns its complexity is the right answer sometimes.
why: Simplicity does not guarantee accuracy. Some problems genuinely need more structure, and the argument is about cost rather than correctness.
Correct. Each layer adds cost, latency and failure surface on every run, so it has to earn its place against a simpler alternative.
Explainability is a real benefit but a secondary one. The operational costs are what make this the default posture.
Model choice is independent of orchestration complexity. Any architecture can use any model.

questions.q: A pipeline has a step whose output quality varies and materially affects everything downstream. The best structural addition is:
opts: Run the step twice and keep the longer output
An evaluator step that checks the output against criteria and triggers a retry or escalation
Skip the step when it is slow
Ask the user to check it
questions.exp: Add an evaluator that checks the output against explicit criteria and triggers a retry or escalation. The criteria are what make it a check rather than another opinion - without them you get an impression, and impressions do not gate reliably. Placing it at the variable step keeps failures local instead of letting them propagate into everything downstream, which is exactly the problem described. Keeping the longer of two outputs uses length as a quality proxy, which it is not. Skipping the step when slow removes it precisely when the system is under pressure.
why: Length is not a quality signal, and running twice measures consistency rather than correctness - two wrong outputs can agree.
Correct. An evaluator checking against explicit criteria, triggering a retry or escalation so failures stay local.
Skipping a materially important step under load degrades output exactly when the system is already struggling.
Manual checking does not scale and puts a person in the path of every run, which is what the pipeline exists to avoid.

questions.q: The clearest sign an orchestration has become too complex is:
opts: It uses more than one model
Failures are hard to attribute to a specific step, and changes have unpredictable effects
It has more than three prompts
It costs more than last month
questions.exp: The signal is diagnostic: when a failure cannot be attributed to a step and a change has effects you did not predict, the system has more coupling than anyone is holding in their head. That is what makes complexity costly - not the component count, but the loss of the ability to reason about the whole. Model count, prompt count and monthly cost are all scale measures rather than complexity ones. A five-prompt pipeline where every failure is traceable is healthier than a three-prompt one where nobody can explain last week's regression.
why: Using several models is a normal cost-and-capability decision that says nothing about whether the system is understandable.
Correct. Unattributable failures and unpredictable change effects mean the coupling exceeds what anyone can reason about.
Prompt count measures size rather than complexity. A larger pipeline where failures are traceable is in better shape.
Cost tracks usage and scale. A system can get more expensive while remaining perfectly comprehensible.

questions.q: The main reason to commit a project-level instructions file for Claude Code is:
opts: It makes the model faster
Conventions, commands, and constraints apply consistently for everyone on the repository
It replaces code review
It stores API keys conveniently
questions.exp: A committed instructions file makes conventions, commands and constraints apply to everyone working in the repository, automatically and identically. That is the whole benefit: it moves shared context out of individual habits and into the repository, where review applies to changes and new contributors get it for free. It does not make anything faster, it does not replace code review - a reviewer still checks the change rather than the instructions - and it must never hold credentials, since it is checked in and visible to everyone with repository access.
why: Instructions shape behaviour rather than performance. Response speed is unaffected.
Correct. Conventions, commands and constraints apply consistently for everyone, with changes reviewed like any other repository change.
It informs how work is done. A reviewer still has to check the resulting change on its own merits.
It is checked in and visible to everyone with repository access, which makes it the wrong place for any credential.

questions.q: Running an agentic coding workflow in CI, the most important guardrail is:
opts: Giving it the largest model
Scoping what it may change and requiring review before anything merges
Letting it run without a time limit
Disabling tests to avoid false failures
questions.exp: Scope what may change and require review before anything merges. Headless CI removes the human from the loop during execution, so the review moves to the boundary and the permissions have to assume something unintended may happen. That reasoning is independent of how reliable the agent has been, because CI often runs against untrusted input - pull request contents are attacker-influenced in an open repository, which makes a scoped blast radius a security control rather than tidiness. A larger model is not a guardrail, and removing time limits or tests removes the two signals that catch a run going wrong.
why: Capability is not a safety control. A more capable model executes a mistaken plan more effectively.
Correct. Scope what it may change and require review before merge, so the blast radius is bounded and a human still approves.
No time limit means a stuck or looping run consumes budget indefinitely with nothing to stop it.
Tests are the signal that catches an incorrect change. Disabling them removes the check that matters most here.

questions.q: A coding agent makes a sweeping refactor when a narrow fix was wanted. The most effective correction is:
opts: Use a smaller model
State the scope explicitly — which files may change and what must not — and ask for the minimal diff
Run it again and hope
Accept the refactor
questions.exp: State the scope explicitly - which files may change, what must not, and that you want the minimal diff. Sweeping refactors usually come from an underspecified request rather than an overeager model: absent a boundary, improving the surrounding code looks like doing the job well. Being explicit about the boundary is both the fix and the thing worth building into your standing instructions. A smaller model produces a less capable version of the same unscoped change, rerunning resamples the same ambiguity, and accepting the refactor takes on review burden you did not ask for.
why: A smaller model makes the same unscoped change less capably. The missing constraint is in the request.
Correct. Name the files that may change, what must not, and ask for the minimal diff - the boundary is what was missing.
Rerunning resamples the same ambiguous request, so a different sweeping change is the likely outcome.
Accepting it takes on unrequested review burden and normalises scope creep in future runs.

questions.q: The best first step when adopting agentic coding on a large legacy codebase is:
opts: Ask it to modernize everything at once
Start with well-tested, well-bounded areas where correctness is verifiable quickly
Disable the test suite for speed
Give it write access to production
questions.exp: Start where correctness is quickly verifiable: well-tested, well-bounded areas. That gives you a fast feedback loop while you are still learning where the tool is reliable, and it keeps early mistakes cheap and visible. On a legacy codebase that property is scarce, which is exactly why you spend it deliberately. Modernising everything at once maximises blast radius at the moment of least understanding. Disabling tests removes the verification that makes the approach safe, and production write access is the opposite of a bounded first step.
why: A sweeping change is the largest possible blast radius at the point when you understand the tool least.
Correct. Well-tested, well-bounded areas give fast verification while you are still learning where it is reliable.
Tests are the fast feedback that makes this approach safe. Removing them removes the reason it works.
Production write access is the opposite of a bounded first step, and nothing about early adoption justifies it.

questions.q: Version-controlling the prompts and instructions that drive a coding workflow matters mainly because:
opts: It reduces token usage
Behavior changes become reviewable and revertible like any other change
It is required by the tool
It makes onboarding slower
questions.exp: Prompts that drive a workflow are behaviour, so versioning makes changes reviewable and revertible like any other change - you can see what altered, discuss it before it ships, and roll back cleanly when a regression appears. Without that, behaviour changes silently and nobody can reconstruct what was different last Tuesday. It does not reduce token usage, it is not a tool requirement, and it speeds onboarding rather than slowing it, since the current instructions are discoverable in the repository rather than in someone's memory.
why: Version control tracks changes without altering what is sent. Token usage is unaffected.
Correct. Behaviour changes become reviewable and revertible, so a regression can be identified and rolled back cleanly.
Nothing in the tooling requires it. It is an engineering practice adopted because prompts are behaviour.
It speeds onboarding. The current instructions are discoverable in the repository rather than held in individual memory.

questions.q: Designing a contract between an extraction step and its consumer, the right order is:
opts: Write the prompt, see what comes out, then write a parser
Define the schema first, constrain generation to it, and validate downstream anyway
Ask for markdown and parse headings
Let each consumer parse differently
questions.exp: Define the schema first, constrain generation to it, then validate anyway. Schema-first makes the contract explicit before either side is built, so producer and consumer agree on the shape rather than discovering it. Constraining generation makes conformance a property of the request. Validating downstream covers what schemas cannot: structure is guaranteed, meaning is not, and a semantically wrong value passes every structural check. Writing the prompt first and fitting a parser to whatever emerges inverts the dependency - the contract ends up defined by one sample of the output.
why: This lets one sample of the output define the contract, and the parser then breaks the first time generation drifts.
Correct. Schema first so the contract is explicit, constrained generation so conformance comes from the request, and validation because shape is not meaning.
Markdown is a presentation format. Parsing headings reintroduces exactly the fragility a schema removes.
Per-consumer parsing means every consumer breaks differently on the same change, with no single contract to fix.

questions.q: A schema-constrained step returns structurally valid output with a nonsensical value. This shows that:
opts: Structured outputs are unreliable
Schemas guarantee shape, not meaning — semantic validation is still required
The schema was too strict
The model needs replacing
questions.exp: A schema constrains shape, not meaning. A date range with the end before the start, a negative quantity, an identifier for a record that does not exist - all satisfy a well-formed schema and are still wrong. That is why semantic validation belongs in your code alongside structural constraint, and it is the boundary worth internalising: structured outputs remove parse failures, which is a real and valuable guarantee, and they do not remove the need to check that the values make sense. The output behaved exactly as specified; the specification simply could not express meaning.
why: This is expected behaviour rather than unreliability. Structured outputs delivered precisely what they guarantee.
Correct. Schemas guarantee shape rather than meaning, so semantic validation remains your responsibility.
A stricter schema catches more structural violations but still cannot express whether a value makes sense in context.
The model produced schema-conforming output as instructed. The gap is in what a schema can express.

questions.q: Across many documents you need identical structure. Beyond a schema, the most useful addition is:
opts: A longer system prompt
One or two worked examples showing the structure filled in for edge cases
A higher effort level on every call
Randomizing the prompt to avoid overfitting
questions.exp: Worked examples showing the structure filled in, especially for edge cases. A schema fixes which fields exist; an example fixes how they are populated - level of detail, phrasing conventions, and what to do when something is absent or ambiguous. Those are precisely the decisions that drift across many documents, and they are far easier to demonstrate than to describe. Choose the examples deliberately: they are the strongest signal in a prompt, so an edge case you include defines the handling you get, and one that only shows the easy path teaches the easy path.
why: More prose adds interpretive room. Examples remove it by demonstrating the decisions rather than describing them.
Correct. Worked examples for edge cases fix how fields get populated, which is where drift across many documents comes from.
Raising effort adds reasoning about a convention that was never specified. It does not supply the missing decision.
Deliberate variation works against consistency, which is the property you are trying to achieve.

questions.q: The most reliable way to evolve a prompt that many systems depend on is:
opts: Edit it in place and watch for complaints
Version it, run the change against a regression set, and roll out behind a gate
Only change it during quiet periods
Let each team keep a copy
questions.exp: Version it, test the change against a regression set, and roll out behind a gate. Each part covers a different risk: versioning gives you something to revert to, the regression set tells you whether the change actually helps rather than trading one failure for another, and the gate limits exposure if something was missed. That combination matters more the more systems depend on the prompt, since a silent behaviour change propagates everywhere at once. Editing in place and watching for complaints uses your users as the regression suite, and per-team copies guarantee divergence.
why: This uses your users as the test suite, and complaints arrive slowly, unevenly, and only for failures someone notices.
Correct. Version, test against a regression set, and roll out behind a gate - covering revertibility, evidence and exposure.
Timing a risky change for a quiet period reduces witnesses rather than risk. The change is equally untested.
Per-team copies guarantee divergence, and a shared fix then has to be applied everywhere separately.

questions.q: When a task needs both prose for humans and fields for a system, the cleanest design is:
opts: Ask for prose and regex the fields out
Define one schema containing both the structured fields and a prose field
Run the task twice with different prompts
Ask for prose and let each consumer interpret it
questions.exp: One schema containing both the structured fields and a prose field. The system reads the fields it needs and the human reads the prose, from a single generation that is internally consistent - which is the property two separate runs cannot guarantee, since the narrative and the data can disagree. Extracting fields from prose with a regex reintroduces the parse failures the schema exists to remove, and letting each consumer interpret free text means every consumer breaks differently on the same wording change.
why: Regex over prose reintroduces exactly the parse fragility a schema removes, and it breaks on ordinary rephrasing.
Correct. One schema carrying both the structured fields and a prose field, so the narrative and the data come from a single consistent generation.
Two runs can disagree with each other, so the prose may describe something the fields do not say.
Per-consumer interpretation means each one breaks differently on the same change, with no shared contract.

questions.q: Designing a tool an agent will call unsupervised, the most important property is:
opts: A short name
Narrow scope with clearly described preconditions and failure modes
Returning as much data as possible
Accepting free-form text arguments
questions.exp: Narrow scope with clearly described preconditions and failure modes. An unsupervised tool is called on the model's judgement alone, so the description has to say when it applies and when it does not, and the scope has to bound what a wrong call can do. Those two properties are what make autonomy safe. Returning as much data as possible works against it by flooding the context. Free-form text arguments remove the schema that constrains what can be passed, which is the last structural check before the tool runs.
why: Name length is cosmetic. What matters is whether the description says when the tool applies and what it can do.
Correct. Narrow scope with described preconditions and failure modes, since an unsupervised call rests entirely on the description.
Large responses flood the context window and bury the relevant result, which degrades every subsequent turn.
Free-form arguments remove the schema, which is the last structural check before an unsupervised tool executes.

questions.q: Two tools have overlapping purposes and the agent frequently picks the wrong one. The best fix is:
opts: Delete one arbitrarily
Clarify the descriptions so each states when to use it and when not to, or merge them
Add a third tool to choose between them
Rename them to be similar
questions.exp: Clarify or merge. If two tools genuinely do different things, the descriptions must say when each applies and when it does not - the confusion lives at the boundary between them, so stating the boundary is the fix. If they overlap enough that the distinction is hard to articulate, that is evidence they should be one tool with a parameter. Deleting one arbitrarily loses a capability without diagnosing the problem. A third tool adds another option to a decision already going wrong, and similar names make the confusion worse.
why: Arbitrary deletion loses a capability without addressing why selection is going wrong.
Correct. State when each applies and when it does not, or merge them if the distinction cannot be articulated clearly.
Another tool adds a further option to a decision that is already being made badly.
Similar names increase confusion. Distinguishing them is the goal.

questions.q: A tool returns 5,000 rows when the agent needs a handful. The right change is:
opts: Increase the context window
Add pagination and filtering parameters so the agent requests only what it needs
Summarize the rows with another model call
Accept it as the cost of completeness
questions.exp: Add pagination and filtering so the agent requests only what it needs. Selection belongs in the tool, where code can do it precisely and cheaply, rather than in the context window where five thousand rows crowd out reasoning and get re-paid for on every subsequent turn. A larger window raises the ceiling without addressing the waste. Summarising with another model call pays a second time to discard data you should not have fetched. Accepting it as the cost of completeness misidentifies context as free.
why: A larger window makes the waste affordable for longer without reducing it, and every later turn still carries the rows.
Correct. Pagination and filtering push selection into the tool, where code can do it precisely and cheaply.
A second model call pays again to discard data that should not have been retrieved in the first place.
Context is the scarce resource in an agent loop. Treating it as free is what causes this problem.

questions.q: Exposing internal capabilities through MCP rather than a bespoke integration is most justified when:
opts: Only one client will ever use them
Multiple clients or agents need the same capabilities, now or plausibly later
The team wants to try a new protocol
The capabilities are trivial
questions.exp: Justified when multiple clients or agents need the same capability, now or plausibly later. That is the reuse argument: a server is written once, versioned independently, and consumed by any MCP-aware client, which turns an integration into shared infrastructure. For a single consumer the protocol is overhead - a process boundary, a version to pin, latency you did not need - and an in-app tool is simpler. Wanting to try a protocol is not an architectural reason, and triviality argues against the extra machinery rather than for it.
why: A single consumer does not need a standard interface. The protocol adds a boundary and latency for no reuse benefit.
Correct. Multiple clients or agents needing the same capability, now or plausibly later, which makes it shared infrastructure.
Curiosity is a reason to prototype rather than an architectural justification for production structure.
Trivial capabilities argue against the extra machinery. The overhead is easier to justify for substantial ones.

questions.q: A tool performs an irreversible external action. The architecture should:
opts: Rely on the agent's judgment
Require explicit confirmation, and make the operation idempotent or safely retryable where possible
Retry automatically on any error
Log the action and move on
questions.exp: Require explicit confirmation, and make the operation idempotent or safely retryable where you can. The two work together: confirmation catches the action that should not happen, and idempotency means an uncertain outcome can be retried without doing it twice. That second property matters more than it looks, because a timeout leaves you unable to tell whether the action succeeded - and without idempotency the only options are to risk a duplicate or to leave it unresolved. Automatic retry on any error is precisely how a single irreversible action happens twice.
why: Judgement is not a control, and an agent's action sequence is decided at run time, so it cannot be enumerated in advance.
Correct. Explicit confirmation plus idempotency, so an uncertain outcome can be retried without performing the action twice.
Blind retry on an irreversible action is how it happens twice, and a timeout gives no indication of which.
Logging records what happened afterwards. The irreversible action has already occurred.

questions.q: An agent's context fills during a long task. The right design response is:
opts: Truncate the oldest messages automatically
Compact — summarize decisions and state into a durable note, re-injected as the working record
Start over with a fresh session
Move to a model with a larger window and change nothing else
questions.exp: Compact: summarise the decisions and state that still matter into a durable note, and re-inject that as the working record. What distinguishes it from truncation is that compaction is selective - it keeps what is load-bearing and drops what is superseded, whereas dropping the oldest messages removes exactly the early constraints that usually still apply. Starting over loses everything. Moving to a larger window and changing nothing else buys time rather than fixing the problem: the context still fills, just later, and the same drift arrives with it.
why: Oldest-first truncation removes the early constraints that usually still apply, which is the least selective possible choice.
Correct. Summarise decisions and state into a durable note re-injected as the working record, keeping what is load-bearing.
A fresh session discards the work. Compaction exists precisely to carry the important parts forward.
A larger window delays the problem without addressing it. The context still fills and the same drift follows.

questions.q: The most reliable way to keep critical constraints in force across a long run is:
opts: State them once at the very start
Carry them in a durable structure that is re-injected each cycle
Repeat them in every user message manually
Rely on the model remembering
questions.exp: Carry constraints in a durable structure re-injected each cycle. Anything stated once competes with everything that accumulates afterwards, and in a long run it eventually loses - not dramatically, but by becoming less prominent than more recent material. Re-injection keeps it in force by construction rather than by hope. Manual repetition achieves the same thing while depending on a person doing it every time, which fails the moment attention lapses. Relying on the model to remember is the assumption the question is describing as broken.
why: Stated once, a constraint competes with everything that accumulates after it and gradually stops being prominent.
Correct. A durable structure re-injected each cycle keeps constraints in force by construction rather than by hope.
Manual repetition works while someone remembers to do it, which is not a property you can rely on across a long run.
This is the assumption that fails. Constraints do not persist on their own across a long context.

questions.q: An agent occasionally repeats the same failing action indefinitely. The right safeguard is:
opts: A longer system prompt
Repeated-failure detection with a cap, then escalation to a different strategy or a human
A larger context window
Removing the tool
questions.exp: Detect the repetition, cap it, and escalate. The detection is what makes this efficient - an iteration ceiling alone lets the same failing call burn the entire budget before it fires, whereas noticing three identical failures ends it immediately. Escalation is what makes it recoverable: a different strategy or a human, rather than simply stopping in an undefined state. A longer prompt does not impose a bound, a larger window just holds more of the same failure, and removing the tool discards a capability to solve a control problem.
why: Instructions do not impose a hard bound. The loop can ignore guidance and continue.
Correct. Detect the repetition, cap it, and escalate to a different strategy or a human so the run ends recoverably.
More context holds more of the same repeated failure. It does not stop the repetition.
Removing the tool loses a capability to solve a control-flow problem that guards would fix directly.

questions.q: Retrieved context and the agent's own conclusions should be distinguished because:
opts: It improves formatting
Conflating sourced facts with generated inferences makes errors impossible to trace
It reduces token usage
The API requires it
questions.exp: Keeping sourced facts separate from generated inferences is what makes an error traceable. When they are conflated, a wrong conclusion looks exactly like a retrieved fact, and you cannot tell whether retrieval fetched the wrong passage or reasoning went astray over the right one - which are different bugs with different fixes. That distinction is also what lets you cite sources honestly and show a user which parts of an answer are grounded. It is an architectural property rather than a formatting preference, and it costs no tokens to maintain.
why: This is about traceability rather than presentation. The formatting benefit is incidental.
Correct. Conflating sourced facts with generated inferences makes it impossible to tell a retrieval failure from a reasoning failure.
Labelling provenance costs a trivial number of tokens. The benefit is diagnostic rather than economic.
Nothing in the API requires it. It is a design decision that makes the system debuggable.

questions.q: The best reliability metric for a long-running agent is:
opts: Average tokens per run
The rate of runs that reach a correct, verifiable end state — with partial progress measured separately
Number of tool calls
Total wall-clock time
questions.exp: The rate of runs reaching a correct, verifiable end state is the metric that matters, with partial progress tracked separately so a run that got halfway is not counted as a success or as a total loss. The word verifiable is doing the work: a run that claims completion is not the same as one whose output was checked. The alternatives all measure activity rather than outcome - tokens, tool calls and elapsed time can each move in either direction for good or bad reasons, which makes them useful for cost analysis and useless as a reliability signal.
why: Token consumption is a cost measure. A cheap run that failed and an expensive one that succeeded look similar by this metric.
Correct. The rate of runs reaching a correct, verifiable end state, with partial progress measured separately.
Tool call count measures activity. More calls can mean thorough work or aimless flailing.
Elapsed time reflects task size and latency. A fast failure and a slow success are not distinguished by it.

questions.q: Two agents in a workflow disagree about a fact drawn from different retrieved passages. The right architectural response is:
opts: Let the later agent overwrite the earlier conclusion
Surface the conflict with both sources attached, and resolve it by a defined precedence rule or human judgment
Average the two answers
Retry until they agree
questions.exp: Surface the conflict with both sources attached and resolve it by a defined rule or a person. A disagreement between agents is usually a signal about the corpus - two passages genuinely say different things, or one is stale - and that signal is worth more than a smoothed-over answer. Letting the later agent overwrite makes correctness depend on ordering. Averaging is meaningless for facts; the midpoint of two dates is not a date either of them supports. Retrying until they agree selects for convergence rather than truth, and will happily converge on the wrong answer.
why: Ordering is not authority. Whichever agent happened to run last would decide the answer regardless of which source is better.
Correct. Surface the conflict with both sources attached, then resolve by a defined precedence rule or human judgement.
Averaging is meaningless for facts. A midpoint between two conflicting dates supports neither source.
Retrying until they agree selects for convergence rather than correctness, and will converge on a wrong answer just as readily.

questions.q: A loan approval system requires sequential stages: credit scoring, income verification, and fraud detection. Why choose a deterministic state machine instead of an autonomous loop?
opts: Deterministic workflows enforce strict regulatory auditability and predictable execution order for known business logic
Autonomous loops are prohibited by cloud data centers
State machines make API tokens free
Claude cannot execute more than one prompt per day
questions.exp: A regulated approval process has known stages and a legal requirement to show what happened in what order. A deterministic state machine gives you both: the execution path is fixed and auditable, and every decision point is a place you can point at afterwards. An autonomous loop decides its path at run time, which is exactly the property that makes it unsuitable here - two identical applications could be processed differently and neither run would be reconstructable. Autonomy is valuable where the path genuinely cannot be specified; in a compliance workflow, the path being specified is the point.
why: Correct. Fixed, auditable execution order for known business logic, which is what a regulated approval process requires.
Nothing prohibits autonomous loops at the infrastructure level. The constraint here is regulatory, not physical.
Control flow has no effect on token pricing. Both approaches bill for what they consume.
There is no such limit. The choice is about auditability and predictability rather than throughput.

questions.q: When setting up CLAUDE.md for a Python backend repository, which configuration enables Claude Code to run automated tests reliably?
opts: Document the exact pytest command, virtual environment activation path, and unit test directory
Paste all database credentials into the markdown file
Instruct Claude to delete any test that fails
Copy the entire Git log history into the prompt
questions.exp: Document the exact invocation: the command, the environment activation, and where the tests live. Agentic tooling has to run tests the way your project actually runs them, and a slightly wrong command fails in ways that look like broken code rather than a broken instruction - which is the expensive kind of ambiguity. Being specific here is what turns run the tests from a hope into a reliable step. Never put credentials in this file: it is checked in and visible to everyone with repository access.
why: Correct. The exact command, environment activation and test location, so the tests run the way the project actually runs them.
The file is committed and readable by everyone with repository access, which makes it the worst possible place for credentials.
Deleting failing tests removes the signal that catches incorrect changes, which is the opposite of what tests are for.
Git history is retrievable on demand and would consume enormous context for no benefit.

questions.q: An enterprise RAG application indexes scanned municipal court records. Why must OCR cleanup occur before computing vector embeddings?
opts: Corrupted OCR text causes embedding drift and leads to high semantic retrieval miss rates
Vector databases crash when encountering misspelled words
Claude refuses to read files that contain punctuation
Embedding models charge higher fees for misspelled text
questions.exp: Embeddings encode whatever text they are given, so OCR errors become part of the vector. A passage full of misrecognised characters lands somewhere unrelated in the vector space, and the retrieval simply never surfaces it - the failure is silent, which is what makes it dangerous. Nothing errors and no one notices; the answer is just missing a source it should have had. Cleaning before embedding is cheap compared with re-indexing a corpus later, and scanned records are exactly the material where OCR quality varies most.
why: Correct. Corrupted text embeds to the wrong region of the vector space, so relevant passages are silently never retrieved.
Databases store whatever vectors they are given. Misspellings produce poor retrieval rather than crashes.
There is no such refusal. The model reads text with punctuation and errors alike.
Pricing follows token count rather than spelling quality. The cost is in retrieval accuracy, not fees.

questions.q: When an MCP server provides access to Jira bug tickets, what parameter in the tool schema prevents context window overflow?
opts: A mandatory limit parameter capping the maximum number of returned ticket objects
A parameter that turns tickets into video files
A setting that deletes the Jira database
A flag that forces all ticket text into uppercase
questions.exp: A mandatory limit parameter caps how much comes back, which protects the context window from a query that happens to match thousands of tickets. Context is the scarce resource in an agent loop: an oversized result buries the relevant tickets, and every later turn re-pays for carrying them. Making the limit mandatory rather than optional is the design decision - an optional cap is one the model can omit, and it will, on exactly the broad query that most needed it. Pair it with filtering so the agent can narrow rather than merely truncate.
why: Correct. A mandatory cap on returned objects protects the context window from a broad query matching thousands of tickets.
Format conversion is unrelated to result size and would make the tickets harder to read rather than easier.
Destructive operations have no place in a read-oriented lookup tool.
Text casing has no effect on token count or context pressure.

questions.q: A customer support bot receives 100,000 queries per day with a 15,000-token system prompt and policy handbook. How does Prompt Caching reduce operating costs?
opts: Cached prefix blocks receive roughly a tenth of the base input rate on subsequent requests within the 5-minute TTL
Prompt caching makes output tokens free
Prompt caching converts requests into offline batch jobs
Prompt caching replaces Claude with an SQL database
questions.exp: Caching turns the repeated prefix into a cheap read. A 15,000-token system prompt and handbook is identical on every one of those 100,000 daily calls, and without caching it is billed in full each time; cached reads cost roughly a tenth of the base input rate, so the saving at that volume is the dominant cost lever available. Two conditions make it work: the stable content must come first, because caching is a prefix match, and traffic must be frequent enough to stay within the TTL - which at 100,000 queries a day it comfortably is.
why: Correct. The repeated prefix is served at roughly a tenth of the base input rate instead of being billed in full on every call.
Caching applies to input. Output tokens are billed normally regardless.
Batch processing is a separate mechanism with its own discount and latency profile. Caching does not convert requests into batch jobs.
Caching stores a processed prefix. Nothing is replaced by a database.

questions.q: In an Evaluator-Optimizer loop generating SQL queries, what pre-execution check prevents catastrophic data loss?
opts: Static SQL AST validation ensuring only read-only SELECT queries are executed without DROP or DELETE keywords
Verifying that the query contains at least 50 lines of comments
Checking that the SQL query is written in French
Running the query on the production master database as root
questions.exp: Validate the query before it runs, structurally rather than by inspection: parse it and confirm it is a read-only statement, rejecting anything that mutates. That is a check code can make with certainty, which is what you want in front of an irreversible operation - the model generating the SQL is the thing you are guarding against, so its judgement cannot be the guard. Pair it with a read-only connection to a replica, so the permission and the validation both have to fail before anything is lost.
why: Correct. Parse and validate that only read-only statements execute, which is a check code can make with certainty.
Comment volume says nothing about whether a query is destructive. A well-commented DELETE is still a DELETE.
Language of the comments is irrelevant to what the query does.
Running generated SQL as root on production is the exact scenario the check exists to prevent.

questions.q: How does Claude Code resolve Git merge conflicts across multiple source code files during autonomous development?
opts: It parses the merge conflict markers, analyzes the functional intent of both branches, writes the reconciled code, and runs tests
It deletes all conflicted files from the repository
It renames all branch files to .backup and halts
It automatically selects the incoming branch for every change
questions.exp: The useful behaviour is to read both sides, work out what each branch was trying to achieve, write code that satisfies both intents, and then run the tests. The last step is what makes it trustworthy - a reconciliation that compiles is not necessarily correct, and tests are the evidence. Note this is a capability to supervise rather than to trust blindly: merge conflicts are exactly where two people's assumptions collide, and a plausible reconciliation can quietly drop one side's intent. Review the resulting diff.
why: Correct. Read both sides, reconcile the functional intent, then run the tests - the verification is what makes it trustworthy.
Deleting conflicted files discards work from both branches, which is data loss rather than resolution.
Renaming and halting defers the problem without attempting the reconciliation.

Architect Foundations assumes you're comfortable with everything in the Developer cert — the Messages API, tool use, the basic agent loop, and MCP at a conceptual level. If those feel shaky, it's worth a detour through the Developer study guide first. What's new here is the shift in vantage point: instead of 'how do I write the code for one agent,' the question becomes 'given a business problem, what's the right shape of system, and why.'

The architect's core question

Every scenario in this cert is really asking the same thing in different clothes: what is the simplest system that reliably solves this problem, and where exactly does it become unreliable? Architecture is fundamentally about trade-offs — more orchestration buys capability but costs latency, money, and new failure modes; less orchestration is cheap and fast but breaks on anything the fixed path didn't anticipate. Good architects can articulate exactly where that line sits for a given problem, not just default to 'more agents' or 'fewer agents.'

A note on scenario-based study

Architect-level questions tend to arrive wrapped in a business scenario — customer support agents, code generation with Claude Code, multi-agent research, developer productivity, CI pipelines, structured data extraction. The same underlying knowledge — orchestration patterns, tool design, context management — gets tested through different business framings, so learning the patterns deeply matters far more than memorizing any one scenario. For the actual exam format, see the official exam guide in Partner Academy.

  • Every scenario reduces to: what's the simplest reliable architecture, and where does it break?
