🏛️ Architect Foundations: Topology Selection Matrix

The Certified Architect Foundations (CCAR-F) exam evaluates your ability to design robust, scalable, and cost-effective AI solutions. Choosing the wrong architectural topology is the #1 cause of project failure.

TopologyExecution FlowBest Use CaseExam Trigger Keyword
Prompt ChainingDeterministic Sequential (A → B → C)Fixed business pipelines, ETL"Step-by-step verified workflow"
Router PatternClassifier → Specialist PromptCustomer intent routing"Diverse inbound query types"
Orchestrator-WorkersCentral planner → Parallel workersDocument processing, research"Parallel independent subtasks"
Evaluator-OptimizerGenerator ↔ Rubric Grader LoopHigh-precision code/writing"Iterative refinement until threshold"
Autonomous AgentModel-directed tool execution loopOpen-ended goal resolution"Dynamic problem solving with tools"

Architecture here means choosing the shape of the system, and Anthropic's own guidance is explicit: use the simplest pattern that works, and escalate complexity only when the task demands it. Every additional layer adds cost, latency, and failure surface.

Climb this ladder only as far as the task actually requires.

The patterns, simplest first

  • Single call — one well-specified request. Most tasks stop here.
  • Prompt chaining / fixed workflow — known steps in a known order, with tool calls at defined points. The right answer for predictable sequences such as look up order, check policy, draft refund.
  • Routing — a classifier dispatches to specialist handlers. Each handler gets a focused prompt and tool set, improving quality and cost per query type.
  • Evaluator-optimiser — a generate step plus a check step with defined criteria and a retry or escalation path. Use where one step's quality varies and everything downstream depends on it.
  • Orchestrator-workers — separable subtasks explored in parallel, then synthesised. Justified when subtasks are genuinely independent and benefit from isolated contexts.

Autonomy is a spectrum, not a switch

An agent decides its own steps; a workflow follows yours. Sensitive or irreversible actions — deleting data, sending mail, moving money — require human confirmation regardless of how autonomous the surrounding system is. Autonomy is about who chooses the path, never about who approves consequences.

Bounding loops

Agent loops occasionally spiral, repeating a failing action indefinitely. The architectural fix is loop guards: maximum iterations, repeated-failure detection, budget caps, and an escalation or fallback path. A more capable model does not create a termination condition, and removing the tool is disproportionate to a retry bug.

Knowing when it is too complex

The practical ceiling is diagnosability. When failures can no longer be attributed to a specific step, and changes have unpredictable effects, the system has outgrown its design — regardless of how many models or prompts it happens to use.

Picking the pattern
Predictable sequence, tools at known points -> fixed workflow
Three query types, different handling       -> routing
One variable step gates everything after it -> evaluator-optimiser
Four independent research questions         -> orchestrator-workers
Steps unknowable until run time             -> agent loop + guards
Key takeaways
  • Use the simplest pattern that works; escalate only on demonstrated need.
  • Fixed workflows beat agents whenever the path is predictable.
  • Routing gives each category a focused prompt and tool set.
  • Irreversible actions need human confirmation at any autonomy level.
  • Loop guards — caps, failure detection, budgets, escalation — are mandatory.
  • Loss of failure attribution is the real complexity ceiling.
Common pitfalls

Reaching for multi-agent first. More agents means more cost, latency, and failure surface — not automatically more capability.

Voting or debating on a task with a known path. It multiplies cost to reach an answer a workflow would have produced directly.

🔍 Enterprise 3-Tier Hybrid RAG Architecture

Production enterprise search cannot rely on dense vector embeddings alone. Hybrid RAG combines Dense Vector Search (semantic concepts) with Sparse BM25 Search (exact keywords, error codes, SKUs), scored via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and filtered by a Cross-Encoder Re-Ranker.

RRF Score Formula:
RRF_Score(document) = Sum [ 1.0 / (60 + Dense_Rank) + 1.0 / (60 + BM25_Rank) ]

⚠️ Table Fragmentation & Contextual Headers

Never split markdown or HTML tables across arbitrary chunk boundaries. Always implement Semantic Chunking that keeps tables intact, and prepend document hierarchy headers (e.g. [Document: 10-K > Section: Q3 Revenue]) to every chunk before embedding.

Agentic coding is structured work, not a single sweeping instruction. The architect's job is to make the agent's behaviour consistent across a team, bounded in what it may change, and verifiable before anything merges.

The recommended Claude Code loop for non-trivial changes — verify gates every execute step.

Project instructions as shared configuration

A checked-in project instructions file — conventions, commands, guardrails — applies the same rules to every engineer on the repository. Verbal norms are neither discoverable nor enforceable, and private notes guarantee divergence. Because it is committed, it is reviewable and revertible like any other change. Secrets never belong in it.

Plan, then execute in verified steps

For anything substantial, explore and plan first, review the plan, then execute in steps with verification — tests — between them. A single 'refactor everything' prompt produces an unreviewable change. Tests are the mechanism that makes agentic edits safe, so disabling them to move faster removes the only signal that matters.

Scope is an instruction

When an agent makes a sweeping change where a narrow fix was wanted, the usual cause is that no boundary was stated. Say which files may change, what must not, and ask for the minimal diff. Unstated scope is inferred scope.

Subagents

Subagents run work in separate context windows, keeping the main session focused and enabling parallel work. They share the same models and the same permissions — the benefit is isolation, not capability or privilege.

Automating the quality gate

To have tests run before work is declared done, encode the requirement in the project instructions or enforce it with hooks. Relying on the agent to remember is not a mechanism.

Headless use in CI

Running agentic coding unattended in CI demands scoped permissions, no direct push to the main branch, and changes landing as diffs a human reviews. Auto-merging anything green removes the review that made it safe; running as repository admin gives the widest possible blast radius.

A safe CI setup
trigger      pull request only
permissions  read repo, write branch; never push to main
scope        lint and formatting paths only
verify       full test suite must pass
output       PR diff for human review, no auto-merge
Key takeaways
  • Commit project instructions so conventions apply to everyone and stay reviewable.
  • Plan, review the plan, then execute in steps with tests between.
  • State the allowed scope explicitly and ask for the minimal diff.
  • Subagents buy context isolation and parallelism, not extra privilege.
  • Encode the test requirement in instructions or hooks, not in trust.
  • In CI: scoped permissions, no push to main, human-reviewed diffs.
Common pitfalls

Starting on the least understood part of a legacy codebase. Begin where tests make correctness verifiable quickly.

Letting it run unattended overnight. Unreviewed volume is not progress.

🧱 The 80% Context Management Rule & Headroom Preservation

Context is a shared finite resource (1M tokens on current Opus and Sonnet models). System instructions, tool definitions, RAG documents, and conversation history all compete for the same window. You must trigger semantic compaction proactively at 80% capacity (160,000 tokens) to guarantee adequate headroom for the compaction prompt and response generation.

At architect level, prompting is contract design. The question is not how to phrase a request but what interface each step exposes to the next, and how that interface is enforced.

Evaluator-optimizer loop — trades tokens for quality, use where it's worth it.

Contract first

Define the schema, constrain generation to it, and validate downstream anyway. On current models that means structured outputs — a schema through output_config.format, or a tool with a strict input schema. Reverse-engineering a contract from observed output is fragile, and free-form text with a regex parser is the pattern this replaces.

Outdated technique

Older material teaches prefilling the assistant turn with { to force JSON. Current Claude models reject a prefilled final assistant turn with a 400 error.

Shape is not meaning

A schema-constrained step can return structurally valid output containing a nonsensical value — an end date before a start date, a negative quantity. That is the mechanism working as specified. Semantic validation stays your responsibility, and returning a clear, actionable error lets the model correct itself on the next turn.

Examples carry what schemas cannot

Schemas express structure; they cannot express convention or judgment about edge cases. One or two worked examples showing the structure filled in — particularly for awkward inputs — communicate expectations a schema has no way to encode.

Prompts as shared infrastructure

When forty prompts must share a tone or policy, copy-paste guarantees the copies drift. Use a shared, versioned system-prompt component included by all of them. Evolving a prompt many systems depend on means versioning it, running the change against a regression set, and rolling out behind a gate — not editing in place and waiting for complaints.

Serving humans and machines at once

When a task must produce prose for people and fields for a system, define one schema containing both rather than generating twice or parsing prose after the fact. One generation, both consumers, guaranteed consistent.

One contract, two consumers
{
  "risk_level": "high",          // for routing logic
  "confidence": 0.82,            // for thresholding
  "summary": "...",              // for the human reviewer
  "evidence": ["...", "..."]     // for audit
}

Generated once against a single schema, so the prose and the fields can never disagree.

Key takeaways
  • Define the schema first, constrain generation to it, validate anyway.
  • Structured outputs replace prefilling, which errors on current models.
  • Schemas guarantee shape, never semantics.
  • Return actionable errors so the model can self-correct next turn.
  • Examples encode conventions and edge cases that schemas cannot.
  • Share one versioned prompt component rather than forty copies.
Common pitfalls

Asking for 'mostly JSON'. Not a contract anything can depend on.

Loosening a schema so it stops failing. That widens the range of bad input rather than fixing the cause.

🎯 Exam Tip — Few-Shot Example Anchor

Providing 1-3 worked examples (few-shot prompting) is the single most effective way to pin down complex output structure across diverse edge cases.

Tools are the agent's interface to the world, and their design determines how often it does the right thing. A tool an agent calls unsupervised must be easy to select correctly, hard to misuse, and clear when it fails.

Fewer, sharper tools beat many overlapping ones.

Few, distinct, well described

Prefer a small number of well-named tools with distinct purposes and strict schemas over many overlapping micro-tools. Descriptions should state when a tool applies and when it does not — selection errors are usually description problems. A generic do-anything endpoint destroys the model's ability to choose correctly, and terse names strip out the information it chooses on.

Protect the context window

A tool that can return ten thousand rows when the agent needs a handful should support filtering and pagination and return concise results. Filtering at the source beats paying to carry data into context and then discarding it. Failing hard above an arbitrary limit makes the tool unusable for legitimate queries; returning a bare file path just moves the work elsewhere.

Design for safe failure

Validate semantics inside the tool and return errors the model can act on. For irreversible external actions, require explicit confirmation and make the operation idempotent or safely retryable where possible, so a retry after an ambiguous timeout cannot double-apply it.

When MCP earns its place

Wrap a capability as an MCP server when multiple clients or agents should reuse it through a standard interface. With one permanent consumer the indirection may not pay for itself, and a protocol hop will not beat an in-process call on latency.

Least privilege at the server

A server exposing SQL for analytics should offer read-only access to a replica, query allowlists and limits, and audit logging. Not production read-write, and never root credentials — the model being careful is not a security control. Descriptions supplied by a third-party server are untrusted content and must not be able to escalate what the agent may do.

Two designs for the same capability
Weak:   run_sql(query)             // full access, unbounded result
Better: search_orders(customer_id, status?, since?, limit=20)
        - read-only replica
        - allowlisted columns
        - paginated, capped
        - documented: when to use, when not to
Key takeaways
  • Few distinct tools with strict schemas beat many overlapping ones.
  • Descriptions must say when a tool applies and when it does not.
  • Support filtering and pagination; protect the context window at the source.
  • Confirm irreversible actions; make them idempotent where possible.
  • MCP pays off when several clients reuse the capability.
  • Least privilege at the server: read-only replicas, allowlists, audit logs.
Common pitfalls

Deleting a tool to fix mis-selection. Sharpen both descriptions instead — that is where the ambiguity lives.

Trusting a connected server's descriptions. Permissions are enforced by your application, not by what a description claims.

Context is the scarcest resource in a long-running agent, and reliability is mostly the discipline of deciding what survives. Everything competes for the same window: instructions, tool results, retrieved material, and the record of what has already been decided.

Compact before context erosion causes forgotten constraints, not after.

Compaction over truncation

As a run grows, early constraints get crowded out. Compaction periodically summarises decisions and state into a durable note that is re-injected as the working record. Blind truncation discards by position rather than importance, so it drops whatever happens to be oldest — often the constraints that mattered most. Compact proactively at a utilisation threshold, leaving headroom to perform the summarisation itself.

Just-in-time retrieval

When a corpus far exceeds the window and most content is irrelevant per query, retrieve rather than preload. Preloading is only sensible when the material is small enough that selecting from it costs more than carrying it.

Keep provenance separate

Distinguish retrieved facts from the agent's own conclusions. Conflating sourced material with generated inference makes errors impossible to trace, and when two sources disagree the conflict should be surfaced with both attached rather than resolved silently by recency.

Deterministic work belongs in code

Date arithmetic, exact totals, identifier validation — let the model orchestrate and let code compute. Instructions cannot make arithmetic deterministic.

Designing for failure

Model outages and degraded responses are routine at scale. Plan fallbacks: retries with backoff, model fallback tiers, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation paths. Add repeated-failure detection with a cap and a defined escalation so an agent cannot repeat a failing action indefinitely.

Measuring reliability

The metric that matters is the rate of runs reaching a correct, verifiable end state, with partial progress tracked separately. Token counts, tool-call volume, and wall-clock time are diagnostics, not goals.

What survives compaction
KEEP    the goal, hard constraints, decisions taken and why,
        open questions, identifiers and references
DROP    verbatim tool output already summarised,
        superseded drafts, exploratory dead ends
NEVER   silently drop a constraint because it was oldest
Key takeaways
  • Compact by importance; truncation discards by position.
  • Compact proactively with headroom to perform the summarisation.
  • Retrieve just in time when the corpus dwarfs the window.
  • Keep sourced facts distinct from generated conclusions.
  • Put deterministic computation in code, not in instructions.
  • Measure verified end-state success, not tokens or step counts.
Common pitfalls

Passing whole transcripts between agents. Pass distilled structured artifacts; raw history is what makes costs explode.

Waiting for a window failure before compacting. By then there is no room to compact.

RAG Architecture: Hybrid Search & Reranking

Vector search (dense embeddings) alone struggles with exact entity matches like serial numbers, product SKUs, or error codes. Production RAG pipelines use Hybrid Search:

  1. Dense Retrieval: Vector similarity search (e.g. cosine distance) for conceptual semantics.
  2. Sparse Retrieval: BM25 / TF-IDF keyword search for exact term matches.
  3. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) & Cross-Encoder Reranking: Re-ranks top results from both methods before injecting the top-k chunks into Claude's prompt context.

lessons.h: Masterclass: Enterprise Production Hybrid RAG Architecture
lessons.b:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in enterprise production requires far more than basic vector cosine similarity. Production architectures implement a Three-Tier Hybrid RAG Pipeline combining dense vector search, sparse keyword search, and cross-encoder re-ranking.

The 3-Tier Hybrid RAG Pipeline
  1. Dense Vector Search (Semantic): Maps natural language queries to conceptual embedding clusters. Excellent for conceptual questions (e.g. "How do we handle customer returns?").
  2. Sparse BM25 Search (Exact Lexical): Indexes exact keywords, alphanumeric SKUs, error codes, and statutory statute numbers (e.g. "Error 0x80040154" or "Section 404(b)").
  3. Cross-Encoder Re-Ranking (Precision): Jointly scores query-document pairs to eliminate false positives and order top-K candidate passages for Claude's prompt context.

Contextual Chunk Headers & Semantic Boundaries

When text is sliced into chunks, isolated paragraphs lose their parent document context. Production RAG prepends structural metadata headers to every chunk before embedding:

[Document: Enterprise Security Policy > Chapter 4: Data Classification > Section 2: Encryption at Rest]
All production databases storing customer PII must enforce AES-256 encryption with automated KMS key rotation.
Exam Rule: Table Preservation

Never slice midway through Markdown or HTML tables. Slicing rows across chunk splits destroys column headers and leads to catastrophic data hallucination.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)

When merging candidate lists from Dense Vector and Sparse BM25 search engines, standard score normalization fails because embedding cosine similarities and BM25 scores have different distributions. Use Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to blend ranks deterministically:

RRF_Score(d) = Σ [ 1 / (60 + Rank_Dense(d)) + 1 / (60 + Rank_BM25(d)) ]

Semantic Chunking vs Fixed Window Splitting

Fixed character slicing (e.g. every 500 characters) frequently bisects sentences and disrupts logical thoughts. Advanced production pipelines employ Semantic Chunking, splitting on paragraph breaks, Markdown headings, or embedding distance spikes between adjacent sentences. This ensures that every chunk represents a coherent, self-contained concept.

Query Expansion & HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)

When user search queries are short, ambiguous, or phrased as questions (e.g. "Why did my deployment fail yesterday?"), vector similarity against raw documentation chunks yields poor recall because documentation is written declaratively rather than interrogatively. Production architectures solve this using Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE): Claude Haiku 4.5 first generates a hypothetical answer passage, and the embedding of that hypothetical answer is used to retrieve actual source documents.

Additionally, multi-query expansion generates 3-5 paraphrased variations of the user prompt in parallel, searching vector and BM25 indices across all permutations to ensure comprehensive recall across disparate technical vocabularies.

Key takeaways
  • Combine Dense Vector search with Sparse BM25 to capture both conceptual semantics and exact alphanumeric keywords.
  • Cross-encoder re-rankers filter out retrieval noise before context reaches Claude's prompt window.
  • Prepend document title and section hierarchy metadata to every chunk to anchor embedding representations.
  • Use Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to merge disparate ranking scores from vector and keyword search.
  • Implement semantic chunking to avoid splitting coherent sentences across arbitrary character boundaries.

The first fundamental principle of AI system architecture is: Never use an autonomous agent loop where a deterministic workflow or single prompt pipeline is sufficient. Unnecessary autonomy introduces latency, nondeterminism, and high token costs.

The 5 Core Workflow Topologies

  • 1. Prompt Chaining (Sequential Pipeline): Fixed linear series of steps where step N passes validated structured output to step N+1. Best for regulated multi-stage document processing.
  • 2. Routing (Classifier + Specialists): A lightweight classifier (Claude Haiku 4.5) categorizes user intent and dispatches to a targeted specialist prompt with dedicated toolsets.
  • 3. Orchestrator-Workers (Parallel Fan-Out): A central orchestrator breaks a complex goal into independent subtasks, executes worker models in parallel, and synthesizes results.
  • 4. Evaluator-Optimizer Loop: One model generates a candidate solution, and a separate evaluator grades it against a strict rubric, iterating until a quality threshold is reached.
  • 5. Autonomous Agent: Model operates in an open-ended loop, selecting tools and inspecting results until it determines the task is complete.
Exam Trap: Over-Engineering Autonomy

On the Architect exams, questions describing fixed business logic (e.g. loan approval, KYC, invoice parsing) will frequently present an autonomous swarm as a distractor option. The correct answer is always the simplest sufficient deterministic pattern.

Latency Reduction via Parallel Orchestration

When processing multi-section reports, sequentially querying an LLM 5 times results in total clock latency equal to $sum_{i=1}^5 t_i$ (e.g. $5 imes 4 ext{s} = 20 ext{s}$). By orchestrating subtasks in parallel with an Orchestrator-Worker pattern, clock latency drops to $max(t_i) + t_{ ext{synth}} approx 6 ext{s}$, achieving a 70% latency reduction.

Routing Patterns for Cost & Speed Optimization

In high-volume customer support systems, over 60% of inquiries are simple FAQ queries that do not require tool use or expensive frontier reasoning. By placing a fast Claude Haiku 4.5 router at the entry point, simple inquiries are resolved immediately for under $0.001, reserving complex agent workflows exclusively for nuanced edge cases.

State Management & Workflow Resumption

Long-running enterprise workflows (such as legal contract review or multi-stage code migration) can take minutes or hours to complete. Production workflow architectures must persist intermediate state after every execution step into a distributed database (such as PostgreSQL or DynamoDB). If a worker node crashes or an API call experiences a transient failure, the workflow can resume immediately from the latest checkpoint without re-running completed steps.

Always design workflow steps to be idempotent and deterministic. Tag each execution stage with a unique run ID to enable full auditability and step-level replay during debugging sessions.

Key takeaways
  • Always select the simplest sufficient architectural pattern for the task.
  • Parallelize independent subtasks with Orchestrator-Workers to reduce clock latency from sum(t) to max(t).
  • Evaluator-Optimizer loops must enforce hard iteration caps (max 3-5 passes) to prevent runaway execution.
  • Use Routers to direct requests to targeted specialist prompts with minimal tool overhead.
  • Filter high-volume simple inquiries with fast Haiku classifiers before routing to heavier agent tiers.

In enterprise applications, context window capacity is a finite shared budget. System prompts, tool definitions, retrieved RAG context, and accumulating conversation history all compete for the same 200,000-token window.

The 80% Utilization Compaction Rule

Context compaction must be triggered proactively at 80% utilization (160,000 tokens). If you wait until 100% capacity is reached, the context window is completely saturated, leaving zero token headroom to execute the summarization prompt itself.

Compaction vs Truncation

  • Blind FIFO Truncation: Deletes the oldest 50% of messages. This causes severe context amnesia, discarding initial user requirements, authentication tokens, and early constraints.
  • Structured Semantic Compaction: Claude summarizes prior conversation history into a structured <key_facts> state block, preserving critical decisions while discarding conversational filler.
Exam Gotcha: Lost in the Middle Attention Curve

Large language models attend most strongly to the beginning (system prompt) and very end (latest user prompt) of long context windows. Critical operational instructions should always be placed at the very end of the prompt context.

State Snapshotting & Blackboard Retention

Rather than re-summarizing conversational prose repeatedly, enterprise agents maintain a centralized JSON state snapshot (Blackboard). At each turn, only state mutations and active subtask parameters are appended to prompt context, keeping total context usage sub-linear even in 100-turn workflows.

Context Token Budget Allocation

Architects must budget context allocations deliberately:

  • System Prompt & Tools: 10% (up to 20,000 tokens) — Cached prefix.
  • Retrieved RAG Context: 40% (up to 80,000 tokens) — Dynamic top-K passages.
  • Active Working History: 30% (up to 60,000 tokens) — Recent turns and tool results.
  • Safety Buffer & Generation Space: 20% (40,000 tokens) — Compaction trigger margin and max output tokens.

Hierarchical Memory Stores & Vector Scratchpads

For autonomous agents executing extended multi-day or multi-session workflows, accumulating context inside the active prompt window is unsustainable. Enterprise architectures implement Hierarchical Memory Systems:

  • Working Memory (Short-Term): The active 200,000-token prompt context containing immediate system instructions and the current subtask.
  • Episodic Memory (Medium-Term): Structured JSON summaries of past sessions indexed in a fast key-value store like Redis.
  • Semantic Memory (Long-Term): Deep knowledge bases and historical transcripts stored in a vector database for targeted on-demand RAG retrieval.
Key takeaways
  • Trigger context compaction proactively at 80% capacity to ensure sufficient headroom for the compaction call.
  • Use semantic structured compaction to preserve key decisions rather than blind FIFO message truncation.
  • Place critical instructions at the end of prompt contexts to exploit the LLM attention curve.
  • Maintain structured JSON blackboard state to avoid accumulating conversational transcript bloat.
  • Establish formal token budget allocations across system, RAG, history, and generation headroom.

lessons.h: Masterclass: Resilience, Rate Limiting & Graceful Degradation
lessons.b:
Production architectures must be designed for failure. Upstream network drops, HTTP 429 rate limits, and third-party API outages must be handled with token bucket rate limiting, jittered backoff, and tiered degradation cascades.

Exponential Backoff with Full Jitter

When receiving HTTP 429 (Rate Limit) or HTTP 529 (Overloaded), clients must retry using exponential backoff with full jitter to prevent thundering herd server saturation:

t_sleep = random_uniform(0, min(max_backoff, base_backoff × 2^attempt))

The Enterprise Graceful Degradation Cascade

  1. Primary Tier: Claude Sonnet 5 handles the request.
  2. Transient Retry Tier: Up to 2 retries with exponential backoff and full jitter.
  3. Fast Fallback Tier: Claude Haiku 4.5 handles essential classification or extraction.
  4. Cached Static Tier: Serve pre-computed FAQ response or cached data.
  5. Human Escalation: Create an urgent ticket for human specialist review.
Exam Rule: Circuit Breakers

Downstream tools must be protected by Circuit Breakers. If a tool fails 5 consecutive times, trip the circuit to OPEN to fail fast immediately without exhausting server thread pools.

Token Bucket Gateway Throttling

To ensure fair multi-tenant utilization and prevent sudden spikes from exhausting Anthropic API rate limits (TPM / RPM), deploy an API gateway (e.g. Kong, Envoy, or Redis Token Bucket) that meters incoming requests at the enterprise boundary before forwarding to Anthropic.

Designing Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) for Failed Agent Tasks

When an asynchronous worker task exhausts all retries without success, never drop the task silently. Route the failed execution context, error stack trace, and input payload to an encrypted Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). Automated alerts notify engineers, and a secondary triage agent analyzes the root cause failure pattern.

Health Checks, Canary Deployments & Traffic Shifting

When deploying new model versions, updated prompt templates, or modified tool definitions, never perform an immediate 100% cutover. Implement Canary Deployments: route 5% of production traffic to the new prompt/model configuration while monitoring error rates, TTFT, and user feedback signals in real time.

If the canary deployment experiences anomalous latency spikes or elevated refusal rates, automated circuit breakers immediately rollback traffic to the previous stable baseline within seconds, preventing widespread service disruption.

Key takeaways
  • Always apply full jitter to exponential retry backoff to prevent synchronized retry storms.
  • Design multi-tier fallback cascades: Sonnet → Haiku → Cached Response → Human Escalation.
  • Circuit breakers isolate failing downstream dependencies and prevent cascading outages.
  • Deploy token bucket rate limiters at your API gateway to meter requests within upstream TPM caps.
  • Route permanently failed background tasks to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) for inspection.
